Hi Parth,

Heidegger makes a distinction between _Zuhandenheit_ (the ready-to-hand) and _Vorhandenheit_, the present-at-hand. That these are opposites seems clear, but a moment of reflection on something like a hammer is instructive: If all goes well, the hammer disappears from your awareness, but if it breaks or otherwise stops doing what it's supposed to, it takes center stage for a while until it is somehow repaired or replaced. So infrastructure that does its job quietly disappears from our radar, while bad infrastructure makes us pay constant attention, to work around its problems, and to constantly re-jig our plans against the irregularities that it forces on us. In that sense, toolmaking is a craft whose goal is to make things disappear; to allow them to be in a state of _Zuhandenheit_ as much as possible.

These thoughts were brought to mind by running a few models locally with `ollama run`. While I've written some words about these models, the hidden stack that actually delivers those words (quantization decisions, memory management, inference optimization, and so much more) is completely out of sight. The great thing is that it works, that the complexity is withdrawn so all I have to think about is models and their use. One could think of this as a kind of failure of attention. To some extent, perhaps it is, but there's also something very good about being able to work with the models directly without constantly battling with their inner machinery.

Consider the case of my work on inference. Prefill is essentially compute-bound while decode is memory-bandwidth bound. Memory bandwidth is the central bottleneck in the whole system, and one should be able to see the effects of various tradeoffs (better but more memory-intensive models, vocab sizes, and so on) in it. When your task is to take a load of compute capabilities and memory bandwidth and stick them in a box and make sure the result is a piece of software that people can use, you spend a lot of time thinking about how to avoid exceeding a memory bandwidth bottleneck and then how to keep the result from choking on that limit while also handling the rest of the work. You spend a lot of time trying until the model runs fast, or you have to conclude it can't.

To be very clear, I have made a lot of mistakes and find the process hard and challenging. Every day, I am considerably less able to organize my obsession into a coherent plan than I was as a kid.

But I can't help thinking it's impressive, perhaps admirable, that you have remained so closely involved with the material work of building something real from metal and silicon. And to have a strong taste for technical depth without flailing. One of our strongest values is evidenced by willingness to actually think through a problem to its conclusion rather than by bravado and performative problem-solving.

Thank you for going the distance and, yes, keep building.

[^sign]
